strengths: Well-motivated practical problem combining offline RL with delayed deployment dynamics
Strong empirical results on D4RL benchmarks with substantial improvements over baselines (e.g., 88.1 vs 3.1 on Walker2d medium-replay at 16-step delay)
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple data quality levels and both deterministic/stochastic delays
Clear articulation of design choices with concrete justification for belief-based policy iteration over two-stage approaches
Theoretical grounding through lemmas and propositions connecting augmented and belief-based formulations
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: combines existing components (transformer belief from DFBT, policy-constrained RL from BRAC/ReBRAC) in somewhat incremental manner
Significant theoretical gap: Remark 4.5 explicitly admits formal offline sample complexity analysis is missing, undermining efficiency claims
Severely restricted experimental scope: only locomotion tasks tested; authors acknowledge scaling to vision-based manipulation 'remains open'
Critical restrictive assumptions limiting real-world applicability: assumes known delay length Δ, deterministic actuation latency, and cannot handle adaptive/heterogeneous delays

Potentially suboptimal baselines: Belief-CQL fails dramatically without clear analysis; augmentation baselines may be under-tuned; missing comparisons with IQL and online delayed RL methods adapted offline

Missing critical ablations and analyses: no ablation on transformer architecture, impact of λ₁/λ₂ hyperparameters, belief pretraining strategies, or belief prediction error correlation with policy performance
No real-world validation despite motivating the work as sim-to-real problem; only simulation evaluation
Incomplete experimental reporting: single seeds (no error bars/confidence intervals), sparse implementation details, no computational cost analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem combining offline RL and delayed RL challenges in a practically relevant setting
Clear articulation of why naive augmentation and vanilla belief approaches fail, with well-reasoned motivation for the proposed method
Comprehensive experimental evaluation within scope showing consistent improvements, especially on challenging medium-replay datasets
Technically sound belief-based policy iteration framework with theoretical grounding via Lemmas 4.1-4.2 and Proposition 4.3
Integration of transformer belief prediction with policy-constrained offline RL is sensible and produces strong empirical results on tested domains
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (transformer beliefs, policy-constrained offline RL) without new algorithmic insights; the main contribution is engineering integration rather than novel methodology

Significant gaps in theoretical analysis: Lemmas 4.1-4.2 are not new; Proposition 4.3 has limited applicability; acknowledged limitation (Remark 4.5) that sample complexity analysis is an 'open problem' undermines offline RL contributions; MSE divergence approximation departs from theory without justification

Severely narrow experimental scope: only MuJoCo locomotion tasks (no vision, manipulation, or other domains); assumes known delay Δ at deployment; assumes deterministic actuation latency; no comparison with online fine-tuning or warm-starting approaches

Insufficient baseline comparisons: Belief-CQL baseline appears weak (trained on delay-free data); missing comparisons with adapted versions of recent delayed RL methods (DFBT, VDPO, D-SAC); two-stage dismissal is intuitive rather than rigorous; no comparison with uncertainty-aware offline RL methods

Missing critical ablations: no ablation on transformer architecture choices; no analysis of belief prediction accuracy vs. performance; no validation of claimed benefits from 'multiple synthetic samples per transition'; no hyperparameter sensitivity study

Incomplete problem handling: boundary condition treatment with [MASK] tokens is mentioned but underdeveloped; circular buffer approach for variable delays is overly simplistic; claim about 'converting to ordinary MDP' is misleading since method operates in belief space

Reproducibility and clarity issues: belief pretraining details sparse; architectural hyperparameters appear arbitrary; no error bars or statistical significance testing reported; no analysis of belief prediction quality or error propagation; missing computational cost analysis with respect to delay length

Evaluation methodology concerns: unclear if results are single runs or averaged across seeds; no figures showing belief prediction quality on test trajectories; limited analysis of failure modes or approach limitations

strengths: Addresses a practically important and novel problem: training offline on delay-free data for deployment in delayed environments, directly relevant to sim-to-real transfer in robotics
Solid theoretical framework connecting augmented-state and belief-based policy iteration via Wasserstein distance bounds; well-motivated derivation from Lipschitz continuity assumptions

Clear and principled design motivations: explains advantages of belief-based approach over naive augmentation (state dimension reduction) and over frozen belief pipelines (biased targets, distribution mismatch, error drift)

Comprehensive experimental validation with consistent, strong results across deterministic and stochastic delays (4-16 steps), multiple dataset qualities (expert, medium, medium-replay, medium-expert), and three locomotion tasks
Well-executed implementation with practical details (transformer architecture, MASK token handling, online adaptation procedure) and reproducibility materials provided
Clear presentation with good intuitive explanations alongside formal development
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only MuJoCo locomotion tasks, purely simulation-based despite motivating sim-to-real gap. No real robot experiments to validate practical utility of delay-robust policies

Theoretical novelty is incremental: core performance bounds (Lemmas 4.1-4.2) are from prior work [49]; main contribution is application rather than new theory. Remark 4.5 acknowledges formal offline sample-complexity analysis would require restrictive assumptions not holding here
Restrictive assumptions: assumes known delay length Δ at training time (unrealistic—delays often variable/unknown); uniform distribution for stochastic delays only; deterministic actuation latency

Insufficient baseline comparisons: Belief-CQL is a strawman (frozen belief + standard RL); no empirical comparison to other delay-aware methods (D-SAC, DFBT) in offline setting; two-stage alternative mentioned but not fully evaluated

Missing critical ablations: no isolation of component contributions (belief prediction vs constrained PI vs n-step returns); no sensitivity analysis for belief quality, transformer architecture, or regularization coefficients (α, α₁, α₂); MSE approximation of Wasserstein divergence not validated

No analysis of belief quality or error propagation: no study of prediction errors, visualization of learned beliefs, or formal justification for 'richer supervision' claim in stochastic MDPs; transformer architecture choices appear arbitrary
Implementation gaps: construction of augmented behavior policy μ_Δ unclear; n-step returns and Retrace(λ) mentioned but not detailed or ablated; computational costs not analyzed
Scalability concerns acknowledged but not addressed: high-dimensional visual observations likely problematic; no exploration of vision-based tasks despite motivating robotics applications

Experimental presentation: unusual baseline failures (e.g., Belief-CQL ≈ 1.5 on expert tasks) lack explanation; no error bars/confidence intervals; varying performance patterns between deterministic and stochastic settings underexplored

strengths: Novel and practically motivated problem: first work on offline-to-online deployment with delays using delay-free data, addressing the sim-to-real gap in robotics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across D4RL benchmarks (AntMaze, MuJoCo, Adroit) with deterministic and stochastic delays under multiple conditions
Clear theoretical framework mapping delayed MDPs to belief-based policy iteration with formal performance bounds (Lemmas 4.1-4.2)
Consistent and strong empirical improvements over augmentation-based methods and naive belief-based baselines on simpler tasks
Thorough ablation studies justifying design choices (transformer architecture, joint training, data availability effects)
Well-written with good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines well-established components (transformer dynamics models, policy-constrained offline RL) without fundamental algorithmic innovation
Poor performance on harder AntMaze tasks (medium-play, large-play) across ALL methods suggests fundamental limitations in handling exploration, inadequately analyzed
Restrictive assumptions requiring known and fixed delays; cannot handle unknown, time-varying, or heterogeneous delays which are common in real systems

Limited theoretical depth: reuses existing performance bounds (Wu et al., 2024b), no convergence guarantees or sample complexity analysis, acknowledges formal bounds need restrictive assumptions not satisfied
Insufficient analysis of failure modes and belief quality: limited investigation into where belief errors accumulate, when policy-belief alignment breaks down, or why harder tasks fail
Scalability concerns: all experiments on low-dimensional environments (~17-28 D), vision-based perception left as future work, computational overhead during training not thoroughly analyzed
Missing important ablations: no study of constraint strength α sensitivity, belief model error propagation analysis, or robustness to delay mismatch between training and testing
Custom baseline implementations (Belief-CQL, Belief-IQL) not from published work make fair comparison difficult; uncertain if augmentation baselines received equal hyperparameter tuning

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem at the intersection of offline RL and delayed control
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple task families (AntMaze, MuJoCo, dexterous manipulation) with both deterministic and stochastic delays
Thoughtful ablation studies examining transformer architecture, data efficiency, joint vs. separate training, and robustness to delay distributions
Clear motivation for why existing approaches (augmentation, separate pipelines) are insufficient
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (transformer beliefs from DFBT, BRAC-style constraints) without significant innovation; theoretical results are attributed to prior work
Critical assumption of known, fixed delays severely limits real-world applicability; unknown/time-varying delays are acknowledged but relegated to future work
Weak results on difficult tasks: all methods including DT-CORL collapse to near-zero performance on AntMaze medium-play and large-play, contradicting claims of strong generalization
Marginal improvements over simpler baselines: Belief-CQL frequently matches or nearly matches DT-CORL performance (e.g., Walker2d-medium: 87.0 vs 87.4), questioning the necessity of joint training

Theoretical gaps: Lipschitz continuity assumptions informally justified; L₂ distance used as surrogate for W₁ divergence without approximation analysis; gap between Eqs. (3)-(4) and practical implementation
Limited statistical rigor: only 3 random seeds, no significance testing, some high-variance results; standard would be ≥5 seeds for top venues
No real-world validation despite claiming to address sim-to-real transfer; all experiments in simulation only
Misleading framing of 'delay-free learning': method requires building augmented states with known delay structure from synchronized data, not truly delay-free
Incomplete comparisons: weak baselines (augmented-CQL/BC not state-of-the-art), insufficient comparison with recent belief-based offline RL methods, no domain randomization baselines
Pre-training sensitivity unexplored: belief model pre-trained separately with no ablation on quality/duration impact on downstream policy learning
Presentation: dense mathematical exposition in Section 4.1; significant gap between theoretical framework and practical implementation; key results relegated to appendices

strengths: Addresses an important and under-addressed problem: learning delay-robust policies from offline delay-free data, highly relevant for sim-to-real robotics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse environments (AntMaze, MuJoCo, Adroit) with systematic variation over delays, data availability, and delay distributions

Thorough ablation studies validating key design choices: transformer architecture (Figures 2-3), joint vs. separate training (Table 5), data scaling (Table 4), robustness to delay distributions (Table 6)
Strong and consistent empirical results showing substantial improvements over baselines (e.g., Table 2 Hopper-medium: 79.4% vs 75.4% for Belief-CQL)
Clear practical insight that joint belief-policy optimization outperforms two-stage pipelines, with concrete explanations (biased value targets, distribution mismatch)
Solid theoretical grounding with clear derivations connecting augmented-state and belief-based policy iteration (Lemmas 4.1-4.2, Proposition 4.3)
Good reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and code release commitment
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Lemmas 4.1-4.2 are citations from prior work; Proposition 4.3 is standard policy improvement; Remark 4.5 defers sample complexity bounds as 'open problem'

Restrictive assumption of known, fixed delays limits practical applicability; while stochastic delays U(1,k) are tested, they still require knowing the maximum delay; real systems often have unknown or time-varying delays
No real-world validation despite explicit sim-to-real framing; all experiments are simulation-based (D4RL); practical assumptions (deterministic dynamics, known latency structure) are not validated
Poor scalability: AntMaze medium-play and large-play tasks achieve <4% returns across all methods; paper acknowledges needing 'additional goal-conditioned modifications' but doesn't address this gap
Insufficient analysis of belief error propagation: Figure 2 shows prediction MSE but doesn't connect to downstream value/policy errors; missing sensitivity analysis and failure mode characterization

Limited novelty in belief modeling: standard transformer sequence-to-sequence predictor with no uncertainty estimates or robustness mechanisms; no analysis of when/why belief reconstruction works or fails
Computational cost not thoroughly analyzed: training times reported (2-7 hours) but total cost vs. baselines not compared; belief model overhead relative to pure policy learning unclear

Baseline fairness concerns: Belief-CQL and Belief-IQL are strawman baselines (plugging belief into existing methods); augmented-state methods are newly constructed rather than established; missing comparisons to other modern belief-based delayed RL methods
